rows.name: External spur
rows.teeth: Straight teeth on the outside of each wheel.
rows.use: Simple speed changes in machinery with parallel shafts.
rows.tradeoff: Abrupt tooth engagement can produce noise at higher speeds.
rows.thrust: No axial thrust from ideal straight teeth.
rows.direction: A single external pair turns in opposite directions.

rows.name: Internal spur
rows.teeth: An external pinion meshes with teeth inside a ring.
rows.use: Compact arrangements such as planetary gearing.
rows.tradeoff: Tooth interference and assembly clearance constrain tooth counts and geometry.
rows.thrust: No axial thrust from ideal straight teeth.
rows.direction: A pinion and internal ring turn in the same direction when their axes are fixed.

rows.name: Rack & pinion
rows.teeth: A straight toothed rack meshes with a rotating pinion.
rows.use: Linear positioning, steering and machine travel.
rows.tradeoff: Travel length, backlash and rack support affect the application.
rows.thrust: Depends on whether teeth are straight or helical.
rows.direction: Reversing the pinion reverses rack travel.

rows.name: Helical
rows.teeth: Teeth run at an angle to the shaft axis.
rows.use: Smooth power transmission at higher speeds.
rows.tradeoff: Bearings must accommodate the axial force generated by the helix.
rows.direction: An external parallel-axis pair turns in opposite directions.

rows.name: Double helical / herringbone
rows.teeth: Opposing helices share the same gear; double-helical designs may have a central gap.
rows.use: Heavy power transmission where axial-force balance matters.
rows.tradeoff: Manufacture and alignment are more demanding than for a single helix.
rows.thrust: Opposed helices balance axial thrust under symmetric loading.
rows.direction: An external pair turns in opposite directions.

rows.name: Crossed helical
rows.teeth: Helical gears mesh with nonparallel, nonintersecting axes.
rows.use: Light-duty motion transfer between skew shafts.
rows.tradeoff: Localized contact and sliding limit load capacity.
rows.direction: Depends on shaft arrangement and helix hands.

rows.name: Straight bevel
rows.teeth: Straight teeth lie on conical pitch surfaces.
rows.use: Changing drive direction between intersecting shafts.
rows.tradeoff: Less gradual engagement than spiral bevel teeth.
rows.direction: Shaft angle is a design choice; 90° is common.

rows.name: Spiral bevel
rows.teeth: Curved, angled teeth provide progressive contact on conical surfaces.
rows.use: Smooth angular drives, including many differential arrangements.
rows.tradeoff: Precise alignment and matched geometry are important.
rows.thrust: Axial thrust varies with load, rotation and tooth hand.
rows.direction: Shafts intersect; do not confuse with an offset hypoid pair.

rows.name: Zerol bevel
rows.teeth: Curved bevel teeth have zero mean spiral angle.
rows.use: Angular drives using curved teeth without a mean spiral angle.
rows.thrust: Axial force is still possible; zero spiral angle does not mean zero thrust.

rows.name: Hypoid
rows.teeth: Spiral-like geometry accommodates an offset between shaft axes.
rows.use: Offset drives, notably automotive final drives.
rows.tradeoff: Sliding raises lubrication and heat-management demands.
rows.thrust: Axial and radial bearing loads occur.

rows.name: Worm
rows.teeth: A screw-like worm engages a worm wheel.
rows.use: Compact drives with large speed reduction.
rows.tradeoff: Sliding contact can reduce efficiency and generate heat. Self-locking is not guaranteed.
rows.thrust: Substantial axial force can occur, especially on the worm.
rows.direction: Shafts are commonly at 90° with an offset.
